new:
This paragraph is made to be very hard to read. Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion, though, we know that there's an 80% or better chance that we'll hear the Conclusion before we hear its Supporting idea(s).
So we always read the paragraph on Role and Main Conclusion with a special ear for conclusions in the first sentence. This first sentence doesn't sound like an opinion, so we wouldn't initially know it was the conclusion.
But then the second sentence tells us it was the conclusion, by indicating that now we are trying to support that claim.
This suspect is guilty. This is clear from the fact that the suspect had a motive and that the suspect's fingerprints are on the murder weapon.
The verdict is clear from the facts of the evidence. The conclusion is clear from the facts of the evidence.
The other keyword that's useful here is 'and', which almost always joins two Premises.
So using keywords and knowing the usual tendency of Role and Main Conclusion to put the Conclusion earlier than the Supporting idea(s) are both very useful when it comes to sorting out this paragraph.
In terms of making it more conversational, the first sentence is saying,
"Society won't be able to function in a stable way if the citizens don't have stable goals in terms of what they want out of life / country."
After all, a government won't be able to write policy in ways that help citizens if most citizens are frequently shifting in terms of what goals they aspire to. And obviously a society can only be stable if its laws are helping its citizens be happier.

new: This is sort of a Relative vs. Absolute paradox. Consuming sugar makes the level of unmetabolized sugar in the blood higher than it was before eating sugar. But people who consume a lot of sugar have low average unmetabolized sugar in their blood. Maybe there are certain people whose bodies naturally have very low unmetabolized sugar in the blood. And because their bodies start off with such low blood sugar, they consume more sugar than the rest of us. Consuming that sugar raises their blood sugar from very low to below-average. We could use a similar analogy with LSAT studying. "Practicing Reading Comprehension helps you to increase your score on Reading Comprehension. Yet people who do large amounts of Reading Comprehension practice tend to have below-average scores on the RC section." We could resolve the paradox similarly by saying, "People who are already crushing RC don't need to practice as much. People who are super-struggling with RC are the ones more likely to practice RC. So even though their practice is improving their RC scoring ability, their RC scoring ability is still lower than average".
note: Swapping the Logic Games analogy for Reading Comprehension is right; also corrected the adjacent typo 'they're bodies' to 'their bodies'.

new: This argument says: "Fails two of the three routes to club officer, so not a club officer." That skips the third route, special qualifications, so it is flawed, just not the way the original is. The original argument said "does not meet friendship criteria, so ENEMY": a massive logical leap from "not qualified for A" to "automatically in the worst possible category B." This answer only concludes "not A." No absurd leap. No false dichotomy. Just a different mistake: forgetting an option.
note: Correctly says A is flawed because it ignores 'special qualifications'; replaced the em dash carried over from the old text.

new: This argument is logically sound, not flawed. It states that a plant needs a sunny location AND regular watering to thrive. The spot is not sunny and the plant was not watered regularly, so both necessary conditions are unmet. The conclusion, that this "explains why this plant is not as healthy as it should be," follows reasonably: if both A and B are necessary for C, and both are absent, C should not be expected. The stimulus's flaw was a false dichotomy, leaping from "not friend" to "enemy." This answer contains no such leap; it simply concludes that unmet necessary conditions explain the poor outcome. There is no jump to an opposite extreme category.

new: This argument has a different logical structure from the stimulus. It lists three ways to qualify as a club officer (two years' standing OR committee member OR special qualifications) and concludes that Evelyn cannot be an officer because Evelyn fails the first two. That is flawed, but in a different way: it ignores the third route, since Evelyn might have special qualifications. The flaw in the stimulus was jumping from "fails friendship criteria" to "is an enemy," a false dichotomy between two extreme categories. This answer concludes only that someone is not an officer. There is no leap to an extreme opposite category. It concludes "not-X" from failing some of the routes to X, whereas the stimulus concluded "anti-X" from failing the criteria for X.
